lines.text: The night before opening night. The house is dark. One bare bulb on a stand, the ghost light, glows centre stage.
You have come back for a forgotten script. Behind you, the auditorium doors swing shut. Click. Locked.
Hello? Is anyone still here?
Silence. Then a page drifts down from the fly tower and lands at your feet. The handwriting is old-fashioned and very neat.

Good evening, crew member. I ran the shows in this theatre for fifty years, and I’m not finished yet. Opening night is tomorrow and nothing is ready. Run the show for me tonight, cue by cue, and I’ll open the door.
The ghost light flickers. At the side of the stage, a small blue lamp switches itself on.
You open the prompt book. Every page is covered in pencil: cues, moves, warnings.
Good. Every show is run from the prompt corner, and the prompt book is its bible. First, the lights. The lighting desk is out in the seats, and I’ve locked it with a word every actor knows.
A single pool of cold blue light falls down stage left. In the middle of it, painted on the floor, a number glows.
Lovely. Lonely and cold, just right for the letter scene. Remember that number. Now look at the stage: the set is still in its Act One positions, and the crew have all gone home.
The furniture slides into place. Chalked on the door flat, in the Prompter’s neat hand, is another number.
Now that’s a stage I can work with. But a show is more than its set. Go into the wings, stage right, behind the black legs. The props table is in a terrible state.
Every prop sits in its own taped outline. On the black flat behind the table, someone has chalked a number.
Now no actor will walk on empty-handed. Cross to the other side, stage left. The labels have come off every costume on the rail.
The last label goes on. A laundry tag swings from the end of the rail, with a number stitched on it.
Every actor will be dressed. One last question, and every technician should know the answer: what kind of stage is this? There’s a poster on the wall that might help.
A proscenium arch. The audience look through a frame, like looking at a picture. You know your theatre.
Lights, set, props, costume, staging. That’s your code. The exit is on the left wall.
Across the auditorium, the green exit sign buzzes brighter.
The keypad turns green. The exit door swings open and light floods in from the foyer.
Thank you, crew member. Break a leg tomorrow. And on your way out...
So I should leave the ghost light on?
Always. Every night, in every theatre.
The ghost light flickers twice. Blackout.
Find the prompt book. It’s on the stage manager’s desk with the blue lamp, at the right-hand side of the stage.
Unlock the lighting desk in the seats (bottom left), then follow L X cue 12.
Drag to look right and open the ground plan on the easel at the front. Set the stage for Act Two.
Go into the stage right wing, behind the black curtains on the left-hand side of the stage. Put every prop where it belongs.
Now the stage left wing, behind the curtains on the right-hand side of the stage. Label the costumes on the rail.
Find the poster on the right-hand wall. Drag to look right.
Go to the green exit on the left wall (drag to look left) and enter all five digits: lights, set, props, costume, staging.
Find the prompt book in the prompt corner.
Unlock the lighting desk and set L X cue 12.
Use the ground plan to set the stage for Act Two.
Sort out the props table, in the stage right wing.
Label the costumes on the rail in the stage left wing.
Work out what kind of stage this is.
Enter the code at the exit: lights, set, props, costume, staging.
The ghost light. Theatres leave one burning on an empty stage all night so nobody falls into the orchestra pit. Some say it’s for the ghosts.
The house tabs: the main curtain between the stage and the audience.
Black legs. These narrow curtains hide the wings, so the audience can’t see actors waiting to come on.
The cyclorama (or sike): a big plain cloth at the back of the stage. Light it and it can be any colour of sky.
Black borders: short curtains hanging above the stage to hide the lights and scenery in the flies.
The auditorium. Tonight every seat is empty.
Part of the set. The ground plan says where it should go for Act Two.
The house lights snap on. There are voices in the foyer. It’s morning, and the show has started without you.
The curtain waits for no one. Try again.
